title: Route translation mapping and TLS bottleneck scratchpad
content:
Purpose:
Quick, messy note bucket while chasing a recurring client TLS failure for Private deployments behind our peered VPC. Trying to map how route translation / SNAT interacts with the TLS handshake and whether packet reordering or NAT-mapping churn is producing ALPN/SNI failures or session resume breaks.

Context / symptom:
- Intermittent TLS handshakes fail when on-prem client talks to private deployment control plane (customer-managed VPC peered to Redwood). Failure rate ~3-7% per 1k connections; spikes during sustained bursts.
- Failures show up as TLS alerts on client side (handshake_failure / unexpected_message) and sometimes as early TCP RSTs.
- No cert mismatch in most traces; SNI looks correct in some dumps but missing in others.
- Affected path: onprem -> TGW/Transit -> Redwood peering -> Private gateway -> instance. We suspect SNAT/port reuse at peering border.

Timeline (quick):
2025-10-29 09:12 - First report from SE: login failures for customer A after we pushed peering route propagation change.
2025-10-29 12:03 - Reproduced in lab by generating 500 concurrent TLS clients for 30s; observed ~4% fails.
2025-11-04 - Started this scratchpad while trying directed probes.
2026-02-20 - Added conntrack sampling and tcpdump at peering appliance. Still intermittent.
2026-02-28 - Current status: hypothesis narrowed to ephemeral port reuse + asymmetric reply path + SYN retrans timing.

Commands I ran (ordered roughly):
- iptables / conntrack / netstat checks on the appliance:
  sudo iptables -t nat -L -n -v
  sudo conntrack -L | head -n 200 | grep 10.0.
  sudo ss -s; sudo ss -tn sport = :443

- Packet captures: tcpdump and tshark snippets
  sudo tcpdump -i eth0 host 10.4.2.17 and port 443 -w /tmp/capture.pcap
  tshark -r /tmp/capture.pcap -Y 'tls && tcp.flags.syn==1' -T fields -e ip.src -e ip.dst -e tcp.srcport -e tcp.dstport -e tls.handshake.type

- TLS client reproducer commands:
  for i in `seq 1 1000`; do timeout 5 openssl s_client -connect private-gw:443 -servername api.customer.local </dev/null > /dev/null 2>&1 & done
  # and curl with explicit resolve
  curl --http2 --resolve "api.customer.local:443:10.4.2.17" https://api.customer.local/health -v

- Debug TLS flags:
  openssl s_client -connect private-gw:443 -servername api.customer.local -tlsextdebug -msg -debug

Notable captures / outputs (abbreviated):
- capture A (failed flow):
  Client SYN -> Server SYN+ACK -> Client ACK (3-way OK)
  Client TLS ClientHello visible but server never responds; within 200ms client retransmits ClientHello then gets TCP RST (from an IP that looks like a different SNAT mapping).
  Observed server-side: no corresponding application-level accept logged for the second ClientHello.

- capture B (success flow):
  Clean ClientHello with SNI="api.customer.local"; Server sends ServerHello with ALPN h2, continues.

Hypotheses so far (ranked):
1) SNAT port churn / ephemeral port reuse at gateway causing SYN/ClientHello to be associated with wrong backend connection state. When many clients open/close fast, conntrack table entries age and get reaped and a new 5-tuple may get reused and packets misdelivered.
2) Asymmetric path (reply goes out different NAT device) — replies hit a different SNAT appliance that has no matching conntrack entry and sends RST. This explains RSTs with unexpected source IP.
3) MTU/Fragmentation causing handshake to be dropped mid-ClientHello (less likely; no IP fragmentation seen in pcap).
4) TLS 0-RTT / session resumption corner-case: resume attempts with mismatched SNI or ALPN when middlebox rewrites source IP/ports (observed some 0-RTT ClientHello flags in client side traces).
5) DNS caching mismatch: client resolves internal name to multiple A records and NAT chooses one unavailable backend; but captured SNI and server certificate indicate correct backend used in successful cases, so low priority.

Evidence that supports hypothesis 1/2:
- conntrack logs show entries for many short-lived tcp sessions. Some conntrack entries show timeout ~30s but corresponding packet timestamps show churn faster than that.
- tcpdump on appliance1 shows a ClientHello then no server response; appliance2 (peered) shows an RST with a src-ip that belongs to appliance2 (possible asymmetric).
- netstat on gateway shows ephemeral port reuse frequency spike during load tests.

Quick experiments to run next (ordered):
- Increase conntrack/tcp timeout on peering appliance in lab to 120s, rerun repro. If fail rate drops -> supports conntrack expiry cause.
  sysctl -w net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_established=120
- Pin SNAT to a smaller range to reduce reuse collisions (or expand range depending on allocator).
  iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -s 10.0.0.0/16 -j SNAT --to-source 34.120.0.5-34.120.0.250
- Force symmetric egress path for a small lab segment (ensure return path uses same appliance) and re-run bulk openssl test.
- Add packet-level logging to track 5-tuple -> backend assignment at L4 balancer (log mapping table when a new mapping is created).
- Reproduce with single-client high-rate (keep connection open) vs many short-lived clients to observe difference.
- Run tracepath/traceroute with -M to check for PMTU issues, though not first suspect.

Quick notes on specific commands and what I observed:
- conntrack dump line example:
  tcp 6 431990 ESTABLISHED src=10.4.2.17 dst=34.120.44.9 sport=443 dport=49612 packets=12 bytes=980 src=34.120.44.9 dst=10.4.2.17 sport=49612 dport=443 packets=11 bytes=860 mark=0 use=1
  -> timestamps show these entries being removed shortly after client closed connections in load test.

- openssl s_client sample from failed attempt (truncated):
  CONNECTED(00000003)
  depth=0 C = US, ST = CA, O = Customer, CN = api.customer.local
  verify error:num=20:unable to get local issuer certificate
  ---
  TLS alert received: fatal: handshake_failure

- curl -v output where server resets: 
  * About to connect() to api.customer.local port 443 (#0)
  * Connected to 10.4.2.17 (10.4.2.17) port 443 (#0)
  * TLS 1.3 (IN), TLS handshake, Client hello (1):
  * OpenSSL SSL_connect: SSL_ERROR_SSL in connection to api.customer.local:443 
  * Closing connection 0

Other observations / context:
- Customer had recently enabled client-side session-resume and some libraries send 0-RTT. We saw a couple of ClientHello with early_data extension. If middlebox rewrites port, early_data might be dropped or misassociated.
- Some peering appliances are using heterogeneous NAT implementations (linux conntrack vs vendor blackbox); implementation differences may lead to slightly different 5-tuple aging.

Potential mitigations (short term):
- Increase conntrack timeouts globally for this customer path (risk: more table memory).
- Expand SNAT pool to reduce port reuse probability.
- Rate-limit bursty client open/close behavior via ingress policing at onprem side or at peering to smooth churn.
- Turn off 0-RTT/resume for now for the customer's egress path as a quick beta rollback.

Next immediate actionable items (assignments):
- (Aisha) Add timed conntrack snapshot during repro and upload samples to GH issue (due EOD).
- (Daniel) Try pinning SNAT range in lab, run 5k connection burst, compare fail rate (due +2 days).
- (Maya) Check routing policies in transit gateway for asymmetry; ensure return route passes same NAT appliance (due tomorrow).
- (Ops) Consider temporary increase of conntrack table size for customer peering (ops runbook updated).

Unresolved questions / TODOs:
- Is there any evidence the application or load balancer sees out-of-order packets that cause TLS library to decide handshake failed? Need server-side debug logs correlated by timestamp/5-tuple.
- Can we collect per-NAT-appliance packet counts per ephemeral-port to measure reuse collisions?
- If this is confirmed, longer-term: add sticky NAT mapping (pin port range per flow) or move to per-customer SNAT appliances.

Notes to self: keep captures labeled with appliance hostnames and monotonic timestamps (use -j for tcpdump if available), include conntrack dumps and iptables -t nat rules for each capture window.

Raw artifacts saved: /tmp/route-tls-repro/capture-20260220-ap1.pcap, /tmp/route-tls-repro/conntrack-ap1-20260220.txt, gist: https://gist.github.com/aisha-patel/route-tls-samples (private)

If I get one decisive repro where server sees ClientHello but client sees RST from 'different' IP, that will move hypothesis 2 (asymmetry) to highest priority. For now, conntrack timing + SNAT port reuse is my working lead.

-- Aisha
